title: Ch3: Transport Evolution, QUIC and Summary

questions.q: Which scenario's main challenge for TCP is that many packets are "in flight" at once, so a single loss shuts down the pipeline?
questions.explain: Long, fat pipes have a large bandwidth-delay product, so a huge window of packets is outstanding. When one is lost, TCP's reaction drains that pipeline.

questions.q: Why is standard TCP a poor fit for wireless networks?
choices: Losses caused by noisy links and mobility are treated by TCP as congestion losses, so it cuts its sending rate even though there is no congestion
Wireless links have such long RTTs that TCP's timer can never expire
Wireless traffic is always low-priority background traffic
Wireless links cannot carry TCP segments, only UDP datagrams
questions.explain: TCP reads loss as a sign of congestion. On wireless links, most losses come from noise or mobility, so backing off just wastes capacity.

questions.q: Which scenario/challenge pairings are correct?
choices: Background traffic flows: low-priority TCP flows
Long, fat pipes: latency-sensitive short flows
questions.explain: Wireless networks: loss from noise and mobility that TCP mistakes for congestion. Long, fat pipes: many packets in flight, and one loss shuts down the pipeline.

questions.q: TCP and UDP have been the Internet's main transport protocols for about 40 years. Transport functionality has evolved through specialized TCP "flavors" and by moving transport functions into the application layer on top of UDP.
questions.explain: Both routes have been used: TCP variants for specific scenarios, and application-layer protocols such as QUIC (HTTP/3) that run over UDP.

questions.q: Which transport protocol does HTTP/3 run on top of, now that functions like reliability and congestion control have moved into the application layer?
questions.explain: HTTP/3 = slimmed HTTP/2 + QUIC, running over UDP. QUIC provides the reliability, congestion control and security that TCP and TLS used to provide.

questions.q: Which of these are principles behind transport-layer services?
choices: Routing packets through the network core
questions.explain: The four transport-layer principles are mux/demux, reliable data transfer, flow control and congestion control. UDP and TCP are the Internet's implementations of them. Routing and forwarding happen at the network layer.

questions.q: Which layers make up the network "edge", as opposed to the network "core"?
questions.explain: Application and transport protocols run in end hosts at the edge. The network layer, with its data plane and control plane, takes you into the core.

questions.q: What does the acronym QUIC stand for?
questions.explain: QUIC = Quick UDP Internet Connections.

questions.q: Where does QUIC sit in the protocol stack?
choices: Application layer, on top of UDP
Transport layer, as a replacement for UDP
Application layer, on top of TCP and TLS
questions.explain: QUIC is an application-layer protocol that runs over UDP. It does transport-style work (reliability, congestion control) itself, in the application layer.

questions.q: What is QUIC's main goal?
choices: Provide an unreliable, connectionless datagram service
questions.explain: QUIC was designed to make HTTP faster. It is widely deployed on Google servers and in apps such as Chrome and the mobile YouTube app.

questions.q: What is HTTP/3 made of?
choices: A slimmed-down HTTP/2 plus QUIC, running over UDP and IP
HTTP/2 plus TLS, running over TCP and IP
HTTP/1.1 plus QUIC, running over TCP and IP
QUIC plus TLS, running over TCP and IP
questions.explain: HTTP/2 over TCP stacks HTTP/2 / TLS / TCP / IP. HTTP/3 stacks slimmed HTTP/2 / QUIC / UDP / IP. The slimmed HTTP/2 and QUIC together form HTTP/3.

questions.q: In the traditional HTTP/2-over-TCP stack, which protocols are in the application layer?
questions.explain: HTTP/2 and TLS are application layer, TCP is transport, IP is network. UDP is not in this stack.

questions.q: Which of these does QUIC set up during connection establishment?
choices: A route through the network core
questions.explain: QUIC sets up reliability, congestion control, authentication and encryption state together. Routes and IP addresses are network-layer matters.

questions.q: How many round-trip times does QUIC need to set up its connection state (reliability, congestion control, authentication, encryption)?
choices: Exactly two RTTs: one for a handshake, then one for security
None ever, because UDP is connectionless
questions.explain: QUIC combines the transport and security handshakes, so all of this state is set up in one RTT, or even zero.

questions.q: When several application-level streams are multiplexed over one QUIC connection, what is per-stream and what is shared?
choices: Reliable data transfer and security are per-stream; congestion control is shared by the whole connection
Congestion control is per-stream; reliable data transfer and security are shared
Reliable data transfer, security and congestion control are all shared
Each stream is a separate UDP socket with its own congestion control
questions.explain: Each stream does its own reliable data transfer and security, and one congestion controller covers the whole QUIC connection.

questions.q: A browser sends three HTTP GET requests over one TLS-over-TCP connection (HTTP/1.1). A segment carrying the first GET is lost, but the segments with the second and third GETs arrive. What happens at the server?
choices: The second and third requests are held up until the lost segment is retransmitted, because TCP delivers one in-order byte stream (head-of-line blocking)
The second and third requests go to the application right away, and only the first is delayed
TCP drops the connection and opens a new one for the remaining requests
TLS reorders the requests so they can be processed independently
questions.explain: All the requests share one TCP reliable-data-transfer stream. A gap holds back everything after it, so one loss blocks every request behind it. This is head-of-line (HOL) blocking.

questions.q: In QUIC, a lost packet on one stream does not hold up data on the connection's other streams.
questions.explain: Each stream has its own reliable data transfer, so a loss only stalls its own stream. Streams run in parallel without HOL blocking.

questions.q: QUIC's loss-detection and congestion-control algorithms are entirely new designs with no similarity to TCP's.
questions.explain: QUIC reuses TCP's approaches. Its specification says readers who know TCP's loss detection and congestion control will find algorithms that parallel the well-known TCP ones.

questions.q: A Go-Back-N sender with window size N gets rdt_send(data) when nextseqnum == base + N. What does it do?
choices: Refuses the data, because the window is full
Sends the packet and restarts the timer
Sends the packet and increments base
questions.explain: The sender only sends if nextseqnum < base + N. Otherwise it calls refuse_data(data).

questions.q: When a Go-Back-N sender sends a new packet, when does it start the timer?
choices: Only if base == nextseqnum, i.e., this packet is the oldest unACKed one
Every time a packet is sent
questions.explain: GBN uses one timer, for the oldest unACKed packet. It starts on a send only when nothing else was outstanding (base == nextseqnum).

questions.q: A Go-Back-N sender has base = 5 and nextseqnum = 9 when its timer expires. How many packets does it retransmit?
questions.explain: On timeout it restarts the timer and resends sndpkt[base] through sndpkt[nextseqnum-1], which is packets 5, 6, 7 and 8.

questions.q: A Go-Back-N sender has base = 3 and gets an uncorrupted ACK with acknum = 6. What is the new value of base?
questions.explain: base = getacknum(rcvpkt) + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7. ACKs are cumulative, so packets through 6 are acknowledged.

questions.q: A Go-Back-N sender gets an uncorrupted ACK, and the updated base now equals nextseqnum. What does it do with the timer?
questions.explain: If base == nextseqnum, nothing is outstanding, so it calls stop_timer. Otherwise it restarts the timer for the new oldest unACKed packet.

questions.q: What does a Go-Back-N sender do when it receives a corrupted ACK?
choices: Nothing; it stays in the Wait state
questions.explain: The rdt_rcv && corrupt transition has no action (Λ). Any loss is eventually handled by the timeout.

questions.q: A Go-Back-N receiver has correctly received packets 1, 2 and 3. Packet 4 is lost, then packets 5 and 6 arrive uncorrupted. What does the receiver do?
choices: Discards 5 and 6 and re-sends ACK 3 for each, producing duplicate ACKs
Buffers 5 and 6 and ACKs each one individually
Buffers 5 and 6 and sends a NAK for packet 4
Discards 5 and 6 silently without sending anything
questions.explain: Out-of-order packets are discarded, with no receiver buffering, and the receiver re-ACKs the highest in-order seq # (3). expectedseqnum stays at 4.

questions.q: A Go-Back-N receiver only needs to remember expectedseqnum, because it never buffers out-of-order packets.
questions.explain: Its only state is expectedseqnum (plus the last ACK packet to resend). It always ACKs the highest in-order seq # and discards anything out of order.

questions.q: When a Go-Back-N receiver gets a corrupted packet, it does nothing and sends no ACK.
questions.explain: Any event other than an uncorrupted packet with the expected seq # triggers udt_send(sndpkt). That re-sends the ACK for the highest in-order packet received so far.

questions.q: In the simplified TCP sender, NextSeqNum = 1000 and the application passes down 500 bytes of data. What is NextSeqNum after the segment is created and sent?
questions.explain: The segment gets seq # 1000, then NextSeqNum = NextSeqNum + length(data) = 1000 + 500 = 1500. TCP sequence numbers count bytes.

questions.q: What does the simplified TCP sender do when its timer expires?
choices: Retransmits only the not-yet-ACKed segment with the smallest seq #, then restarts the timer
Retransmits all not-yet-ACKed segments, as Go-Back-N does
Retransmits the most recently sent segment
questions.explain: Unlike GBN, which resends the whole window, this TCP sender resends just the oldest unACKed segment and restarts the timer.

questions.q: SendBase = 92 when an ACK with ACK field value y = 120 arrives at the simplified TCP sender. What is the last byte that is now cumulatively ACKed?
questions.explain: Since y > SendBase, SendBase becomes 120. SendBase - 1 = 119 is the last cumulatively ACKed byte.

questions.q: SendBase = 120 when an ACK with y = 100 arrives at the simplified TCP sender. What happens?
choices: Nothing changes, because y is not greater than SendBase
The segment starting at byte 100 is retransmitted
questions.explain: The sender only acts when y > SendBase. An ACK for data that is already cumulatively acknowledged carries no new information.

questions.q: An ACK advances SendBase in the simplified TCP sender. What happens to the timer?
choices: It is restarted if any segments are still not ACKed; otherwise it is stopped
questions.explain: After updating SendBase: if not-yet-ACKed segments remain, start the timer; else stop it. The single timer always tracks the oldest unACKed segment.

questions.q: If the timer is already running when new data arrives from the application, the simplified TCP sender restarts the timer for the new segment.
questions.explain: It starts the timer only if the timer is not already running. A running timer belongs to an older unACKed segment.

questions.q: In the TCP 3-way handshake FSM, what happens when a client creates a socket to a server (clientSocket = new Socket("hostname", "port number"))?
choices: It goes from closed to SYN sent and sends SYN(seq=x)
It goes from closed to listen
It goes from closed to ESTAB and sends SYN(seq=x)
It goes from listen to SYN rcvd and sends SYNACK
questions.explain: Opening the client socket sends a SYN with the client's initial sequence number x and moves the client to SYN sent.

questions.q: A TCP server in the listen state receives SYN(x). What does it do?
choices: Sends SYNACK(seq=y, ACKnum=x+1), creates a new socket for talking back to the client, and goes to SYN rcvd
Sends ACK(ACKnum=x+1) and goes straight to ESTAB
Sends SYN(seq=y) and goes to SYN sent
Sends FIN and goes to CLOSE_WAIT
questions.explain: The server ACKs the client's SYN, picks its own initial seq # y, and creates the connection socket. It reaches ESTAB only when the client's ACK(y+1) arrives.

questions.q: A client's initial sequence number is x = 300 and the server's is y = 7000. What ACKnum is in the server's SYNACK?
questions.explain: SYNACK(seq=y, ACKnum=x+1) = SYNACK(seq=7000, ACKnum=301).

questions.q: A client's initial sequence number is x = 300 and the server's is y = 7000. What ACKnum is in the client's final ACK of the 3-way handshake?
questions.explain: The client replies to SYNACK(seq=y, ...) with ACK(ACKnum=y+1) = 7001 and enters ESTAB.

questions.q: When a server in SYN rcvd receives ACK(ACKnum=y+1), it moves to ESTAB without sending anything.
questions.explain: The action on that transition is Λ. The handshake is done and both sides are in ESTAB.

questions.q: The client starts closing a TCP connection. In what order does it pass through states?
questions.explain: The client sends FIN (FIN_WAIT_1), gets the server's ACK (FIN_WAIT_2), gets the server's FIN and ACKs it (TIMED_WAIT), then waits 2 × max segment lifetime and goes to CLOSED.

questions.q: The client is the one that closes the connection. In what order does the server pass through states?
questions.explain: The server ACKs the client's FIN (CLOSE_WAIT), later sends its own FIN (LAST_ACK), and closes when the client's final ACK arrives (CLOSED).

questions.q: The client closes its socket and sends a segment with FINbit=1, seq=500. What ACKnum does the server put in its ACK?
questions.explain: The server replies ACKbit=1; ACKnum=x+1 = 501 and enters CLOSE_WAIT.

questions.q: In FIN_WAIT_1, the client can no longer send data but can still receive it.
questions.explain: After clientSocket.close() sends a FIN, the client's sending direction is closed but it can still receive.

questions.q: A server in CLOSE_WAIT, having ACKed the client's FIN, can still send data to the client.
questions.explain: Only the client's direction has closed. The server can keep sending until it sends its own FIN and enters LAST_ACK, after which it can no longer send.

questions.q: How long does the client stay in TIMED_WAIT before entering CLOSED?
choices: Until the server's next FIN arrives
questions.explain: After ACKing the server's FIN (ACKnum=y+1), the client waits 2 × maximum segment lifetime before closing.

questions.q: In the simple sawtooth model of TCP throughput (ignoring slow start), what range does the window size oscillate over? W is the window size at which loss occurs.
questions.explain: The window grows until loss at W, is halved to W/2, and grows again. That gives a sawtooth between W/2 and W, with an average of ¾W.

questions.q: Under the sawtooth model, what is average TCP throughput (W in bytes)?
questions.explain: The average number of in-flight bytes is ¾W, and that many are sent every RTT. So throughput = ¾ · W/RTT.

questions.q: A TCP connection loses a segment whenever its window reaches W = 40,000 bytes, and RTT = 100 ms. Using the sawtooth model, what is the average throughput in bytes/sec?
Which assumptions or definitions underlie the formula avg throughput = ¾ · W/RTT?
choices: The sender always has data to send
W is the window size (in bytes) at which loss occurs
The window grows exponentially the whole time
questions.explain: The model ignores slow start, assumes there is always data to send, and assumes loss happens when the window hits W. That loss is what produces the sawtooth.

questions.q: A TCP connection uses 1500-byte segments over a path with a 100 ms RTT. To reach 10 Gbps, about how many segments must be in flight (throughput × RTT ÷ segment size)?
questions.explain: 10×10^9 bits/s × 0.1 s = 10^9 bits per RTT. Divided by 1500 × 8 = 12,000 bits per segment, that is ≈ 83,333 segments.

questions.q: According to the Mathis formula, TCP throughput = 1.22 · MSS / (RTT · √L). What is throughput inversely proportional to?
choices: RTT and the square root of the segment loss probability L
questions.explain: Throughput grows with MSS, and falls as RTT grows and as √L grows.

questions.q: Use the Mathis formula, throughput = 1.22 · MSS / (RTT · √L), with MSS = 1500 bytes, RTT = 100 ms and loss probability L = 10^-4. What is TCP throughput in bytes/sec?
Using the Mathis formula, what happens to TCP throughput if the segment loss probability L drops by a factor of 4?
questions.explain: Throughput ∝ 1/√L. If L shrinks by 4, √L shrinks by 2, so throughput doubles.

questions.q: Take a long, fat pipe with 1500-byte segments and a 100 ms RTT. Standard TCP can reach 10 Gbps here as long as fewer than about 1 in 1,000 segments are lost.
questions.explain: By the Mathis formula, 10 Gbps needs a loss rate of about L = 2·10^-10, which is very small. That is why there are TCP versions designed for long, high-speed paths.
